text: Lesson one named cost as one of the four dimensions that changes at scale. This lesson makes that concrete with real arithmetic -- a per-request decision that looks free in a code review can turn into a seven-figure line item once multiplied by production volume.

Northbeam's support assistant serves two million requests a day at steady state -- a believable number for a mid-size company's customer-facing AI feature. Each request averages eight hundred input tokens and two hundred output tokens. Run the real numbers at realistic API pricing, and that comes out to over ten thousand dollars a day -- nearly four million dollars a year, at steady state, for a feature that looked basically free when it was a fifty-user pilot processing a handful of requests a day. Nothing changed about the system's logic. Only the volume did.

Now suppose an engineer adds four hundred extra tokens to the system prompt -- a few more examples, a longer style guide, something that would pass code review without a second glance. At Northbeam's volume, that adds twenty-four hundred dollars a day, or eight hundred seventy-six thousand dollars a year. This is exactly why a Staff or Principal engineer's review of a prompt change at this scale has to ask what it costs at real volume -- a question prototype-scale instincts never think to ask, because at prototype scale the answer genuinely doesn't matter.

Cost isn't the only number that needs to be explicit before building. If product has committed to a two-second end-to-end response time, that budget has to be split across every component the request passes through: fifty milliseconds to embed the query, a hundred for vector search, a hundred fifty for re-ranking, twelve hundred for the LLM's time to first token, and five hundred for network and overhead. Writing this down before any of it is built turns a vague goal like 'make it fast' into a concrete number each team can be held to.

Setting these budgets after a system is already built means every fix becomes a redesign -- ripping out a vector database, renegotiating a model choice, rearchitecting a pipeline that was never built with the real constraint in mind. Setting them before building means the constraint shapes the design from the start. That's the practical reason Staff and Principal review happens at the design stage, not just the code-review stage -- by the time code exists, the expensive decisions are usually already locked in.
Next, we turn these budgets into a plan for growth -- capacity planning and forecasting AI workloads.
